clue.text: One boozer drinking like this is sign of pressure

indicators.note: a drinker takes what is in the glass right inside himself, so the short word ends up between the two that surround it

parts.note: one is the single stroke I
'so' is the small word for in this way
a boozer is a bar — the premises, not the drinker

explanation.walkthrough: 'Boozer' means the drinker on the surface and the pub in the wordplay, which is the whole trick of the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: An isobar is the line on a weather map joining places of equal air pressure, so 'sign of pressure' names it as a marking on a chart.

clue.text: Debtor's not raging about one wiping bill

indicators.note: words written about a subject run all the way round it, and these ones have the answer lying inside them

parts.note: the letters run straight on from the S of Debtor's through to the RAG in raging

explanation.walkthrough: A bill is a bird's beak, which is what this gets wiped on; the debtor's temper is decoration over letters that were never disturbed at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A snot rag is blunt slang for a handkerchief, and 'bill' lends a bird's beak to a nose, so the phrase names the thing by the job it does.

clue.text: Offer shop might have on crapper loaf regularly

parts.note: a bog is the coarse British word for a lavatory

indicators.note: at steady intervals means every second letter rather than all of them — take them at that spacing

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of lOaF

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is an acronym you only meet on a shelf label — buy one get one free — and the surface is one long lavatory joke pointing away from the shop.
explanation.definitionFit: BOGOF is the retail trade's acronym for 'buy one get one free', so the definition points at a supermarket promotion by its shop-floor label.

clue.text: Help head to save outstanding sculptures

parts.note: aid sent to a disaster area is relief

indicators.note: the head of a word is the letter it begins with, so only that one letter is taken

parts.note: the letter standing at the head of save

explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' is doing literal work — these figures stand out from the flat stone behind them — while the surface offers it as praise.
explanation.definitionFit: A relief is a carving whose figures project from a flat background, so 'outstanding sculptures' describes them by standing proud of the surface.

clue.text: Time state reviewed hospital food outlets

indicators.note: to review is to go back over something already looked at, and going back over these letters reads them the other way

parts.note: t is the standard abbreviation for time
to state something formally is to aver it
a sanatorium is a SAN, turned round

explanation.walkthrough: 'State' sits between Time and hospital looking like a place on a map, and it is a verb. SAN for a hospital is worth banking — it turns up constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: A taverna is a small Greek restaurant serving food and wine, so 'food outlets' is the flat trade description of what they are.

clue.text: Old volunteers consuming ecstasy and grass

indicators.note: to consume is to take something right inside you, so the letter lands within the word rather than beside it

parts.note: the Territorial Army, TA, is the old name for the Army Reserve
E is the tabloid abbreviation for ecstasy

explanation.walkthrough: Stop reading 'grass' as lawn and the whole clue is drugs: the answer has meant cannabis since the jazz age.
explanation.definitionFit: Grass and tea are both old street names for cannabis, so the definition swaps one piece of slang for another rather than naming a drink.

clue.text: One can served up worker filled with Courage

indicators.note: what is served up in a down clue comes back towards the top, so those letters climb instead of descending

parts.note: one is I and a can is a LAV, and I LAV read upwards is VALI
the crossword's tireless worker is the ant

explanation.walkthrough: Courage is a brewery as well as a virtue, so the capital letter does pub-sign duty in a clue already full of cans and lavatories.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone valiant is brimming with bravery, so 'filled with Courage' is that in plain English — the capital C only dresses it as the brewer.

clue.text: It is people like your mother-in-law …

definitions.note: 'It' is the coy old euphemism for sex, an idea with no plural, while the answer in that sense is only ever plural — the mismatch belongs to the euphemism.
definitions.meaning: the coy old pronoun standing in for sex, avoiding the plain plural word for it
the plural noun for family you acquire by marriage rather than by blood

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries the sentence on into 8 down, which is what lets a clue this short read as half a grumble about the in-laws.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the family — a mother-in-law is a relation by marriage; the other is the polite plural for sex, the same coyness as 'it'.

clue.text: … Nanna upset about ultimately flat English dish?

indicators.note: a household upset leaves everything out of its usual place, and so does an upset word
a coat worn about you goes round the outside, so the jumbled letters wrap the pair that follow
ultimately means at the very end, so it asks for the final letter of the word beside it

parts.note: five letters to be rearranged, and they end up split either side of what goes in
the last letter of flaT
E is the usual abbreviation for English

explanation.walkthrough: Reading on from 7 down, a grandmother in a temper about a flat English dinner is a complete picture — and every word of it is machinery.
explanation.definitionFit: An antenna is the aerial that catches a broadcast, and the domestic one is a satellite dish, so the question mark flags a definition by example.

clue.text: I moon gal travelling around foreign land

indicators.note: someone who wanders about does not end up where they set off, and neither do these letters

parts.note: the eight letters of I MOON GAL in a new order

explanation.walkthrough: Hoskins builds his fodder out of a mooning gal, and a picture that vivid is exactly what stops you counting the letters in front of you.
explanation.definitionFit: Mongolia is the landlocked republic between Russia and China, so 'foreign land' defines it by example — one country standing for any country abroad.

clue.text: Short lad steals old literary novel

indicators.note: cut short means stopping before the end, so the word turns up one letter shy

parts.note: LAD with its last letter cut off

indicators.note: a thief takes a thing into his own keeping, so the word doing the stealing closes round what it takes

parts.note: o is the usual abbreviation for old
lit is the standard short form for literature

explanation.walkthrough: 'Old literary novel' reads as one description of a dusty book, and the seam falls right at the end of it: only the last word is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Nabokov published Lolita in 1955, so 'novel' defines it by example — one famous title standing in for the whole class of thing.

clue.text: Revive soldiers hard peasant knocked over

indicators.note: a thing knocked over lies the other way about, so its letters come out end first

parts.note: the Royal Engineers, RE, are the crossword's standard soldiers
a medieval peasant is a SERF, tipped over
H is the pencil grade for hard

explanation.walkthrough: RE for soldiers and H for hard are two of the most reused abbreviations in cryptics — the Royal Engineers appear whenever troops or sappers are mentioned.
explanation.definitionFit: To refresh someone is to restore their energy, which is what reviving a flagging person means — both point at liveliness returning, not at the dead.

clue.text: Fury? That guy will coast on occasion!

parts.note: that guy will is HE'LL, and an apostrophe is never written into the grid

indicators.note: on occasion means now and then rather than throughout, so the letters are taken now and then — every other one

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters of CoAsT

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark sells 'coast on occasion' as a lazy afternoon by the sea, which is where the every-other-letter instruction hides.
explanation.definitionFit: A hellcat is a savagely bad-tempered woman, and the capitalised Furies of myth were avenging females, so the word answers to either reading.

clue.text: Minister's bill blocked by abstaining English knight

indicators.note: a pipe that is blocked has been stopped up from within, so what follows lodges in the middle

parts.note: a bill pasted on a wall is an ad
someone teetotal is TT
E is the usual abbreviation for English
N is the knight in chess notation

explanation.walkthrough: 'Minister' is a verb here, neither a churchman nor a cabinet member, and the apostrophe-s that follows it means no more than 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: To attend a patient is to minister to them — the old sense of tending to someone's needs, rather than preaching or governing.

clue.text: Uniform infantryman stuffed with large fruit

parts.note: U is Uniform in the radio alphabet

indicators.note: a bird stuffed for the oven is packed from inside, so the letter goes into the middle of the word

parts.note: an American infantryman is a GI
L is the clothing label for large

explanation.walkthrough: Two military words in a row and not a soldier in the answer: the whole parade dissolves into three abbreviations and a citrus.
explanation.definitionFit: The ugli is a Jamaican hybrid of grapefruit and tangerine sold under that trade name, so 'fruit' names it by category.

clue.text: Idiotic PM, I tell old head of state, creates irritability

indicators.note: an idiotic arrangement is one nobody sensible would have chosen, so the order these letters arrive in cannot be trusted

parts.note: seven of the nine letters, taken exactly as printed
the late Queen signed herself ER, Elizabeth Regina — the head of state before this one

explanation.walkthrough: The comma makes the fodder sound like a lecture delivered to a prime minister. ER is worth banking: any old queen in a clue may be asking for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill temper is a settled disposition to snap at people, which is what irritability names — the state, not one outburst of it.

clue.text: Allusion to changes related to an answer?

indicators.note: what changes does not stay as it was, and here it is the order of the letters that will not stay put

parts.note: the ten letters of ALLUSION TO rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: The clue quietly describes itself: an allusion changed into something to do with an answer is what every cryptic clue in the grid is doing.
explanation.definitionFit: Solutional is the adjective made from solution, so it describes whatever pertains to an answer; outside cave geology the word is barely used.

clue.text: Criminal knocks sale for hosiery items

indicators.note: a criminal will not keep to the rules, and letters described that way will not keep to the order they were given

parts.note: the ten letters of KNOCKS SALE in a different order

explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal knocks' reads as a burglary report, so the first word passes for a description of the thief instead of the instruction it really is.
explanation.definitionFit: Ankle socks are the short ones stopping just above the shoe, and hosiery is the trade's collective word for socks, stockings and tights.

clue.text: We might beat The Hammers in Linares, surprisingly

indicators.note: a surprise is what nobody saw coming, and these letters do not come out in the order anyone expects

parts.note: the seven letters of LINARES rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: Linares is a Spanish town famous for its chess tournament, which keeps the sporting surface plausible while its letters do all the work.
explanation.definitionFit: 'The Nailers' is Belper Town's nickname, from the town's nail trade, so the boast sets one hammering side against West Ham.

clue.text: Grease-covered slice of meat dons burnt on the outside

parts.note: meat browned in a hot pan is seared — caught on the outside only

indicators.note: to don a coat is to put it on over yourself, so the single letter ends up wearing the longer word around it

parts.note: a slice off the front of MEAT is its first letter

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the wordplay talk cooking, so nothing announces itself as an instruction; 'dons' is the only word doing a job rather than describing a kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: Something smeared has had a greasy substance wiped across it, so 'grease-covered' names the state the wiping leaves behind.

clue.text: Whip a person who causes great suffering

definitions.meaning: the knotted lash used for flogging

definitions.text: a person who causes great suffering
definitions.meaning: Attila earned a famous epithet meaning 'affliction sent by God' — this half names the affliction itself, not the instrument

explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions with no join between them, which is why the clue reads as one smooth phrase; only the length tells you nothing else is coming.
explanation.definitionFit: The literal sense is the whip used for flogging, and the figurative one moved from the lash to whoever wields it — a tyrant or a plague on others.

clue.text: Horse and colt beset by flipping flatus

indicators.note: to be beset is to have something closing in from every side, so whatever is beset sits inside
to flip a thing is to turn it end over end, so the word comes out the other way round

parts.note: flatus is wind, GAS, turned round
a racecard marks a colt with a small c

explanation.walkthrough: The paddock full of horses is there so that the definition looks like one of them, and 'flipping' passes for mild swearing about the smell.
explanation.definitionFit: Horse and scag are both street names for heroin, so the definition trades one dealer's word for another instead of naming an animal.

clue.text: A quiet writer vacuous Duchess puts on?

parts.note: the clue's own A opens the answer
p is piano, the musician's mark for quiet
the writer here is the implement rather than the author

indicators.note: vacuous means empty-headed, and a word emptied out keeps nothing but the two letters at its ends

parts.note: DucheS emptied of everything between its ends

explanation.walkthrough: 'Puts on' invites you to watch a duchess dressing, when the answer wants the dry office sense of adding a paragraph at the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: To append is to tack something onto the end of what is already there, which is one plain sense of 'puts on' — adding rather than wearing.

clue.text: Cut grass over one trimmed part of garden

indicators.note: a sheet laid over a thing covers it from both sides, so the grass closes round what follows

parts.note: rye is a grass grown as a crop

indicators.note: a trimmed hedge has had its end taken off, and so has this word

parts.note: one is the single stroke I
a BED is part of a garden, with its last letter trimmed off

explanation.walkthrough: Every word belongs to the garden and the clue reads as an afternoon's mowing, right up to the point where 'Cut' turns out to be butchery.
explanation.definitionFit: A ribeye is the steak taken from the rib section, and butchers call any such joint a cut, so the definition names it by trade category.

clue.text: Tumble, being tackled by excellent hooker

indicators.note: a player who is tackled gets wrapped up by whoever tackles him, so the other word closes around this one

parts.note: top marks, top drawer — top means excellent
to tumble down a slope is to roll

explanation.walkthrough: Everything except the definition is rugby, and the definition is the one word that looks most like rugby of all.
explanation.definitionFit: A trollop is a disreputable woman, and 'hooker' is the blunt slang for a prostitute — the same insult in newer dress, not the front-row forward.

clue.text: Reason I will get into record by contralto

indicators.note: to get into a place is to end up inside it, so the letter lands within the pair rather than after them

parts.note: a ship's daily record is its log
the clue's I is used as the letter itself
vocal parts are marked S, C, T and B — C is the contralto

explanation.walkthrough: 'Reason' is the noun, not the verb, and the surface sounds like a singer muscling onto somebody's recording — which is the picture 'get into' was chosen for.
explanation.definitionFit: Logic is the discipline of valid inference, and reason in the sense of sound thinking is a plain synonym for it — not reason meaning a cause.

clue.text: Dutch goalie misses header further down pitch

indicators.note: the header is the letter at the top of the word, and missing it means starting one letter late

parts.note: D is the standard abbreviation for Dutch
a goalie is a KEEPER, and it is the K at the front that goes missing

explanation.walkthrough: A goalkeeper missing a header is ordinary match commentary, and the football runs on one word past the point where the definition has quietly begun.
explanation.definitionFit: A deeper note sits lower on the scale, so 'further down pitch' is the musical reading — the football pitch of the surface is another word entirely.

clue.text: Pubs rung up to get shooters from America

indicators.note: a thing that is up has been stirred out of its settled state, so the letters in front of it will not stay as they were

parts.note: the eight letters of PUBS RUNG in a new order

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rung up' reads as a phone call round the pubs, which hides the fact that only the last of those words is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A burp gun is GI slang for a submachine gun, named for the belching noise of its rapid fire — 'shooters' being the blunt word for firearms.

clue.text: Case of red, say, one put in case of brown

indicators.note: a case is what encloses a thing, so this asks only for the letters at the two ends
to put a thing in is to place it inside something else, so the letter sits within the word

parts.note: the two letters at the ends of BROWN
one is the single stroke I

explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' does two jobs a few words apart — wine storage in the definition, a word's outer shell in the wordplay — and 'say' marks the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A bin is the rack a wine is laid down in, so a container of red is one example of what bins hold, which is what the 'say' flags.

clue.text: A way old academic will describe rare dinosaur

indicators.note: to describe a circle in geometry is to draw it round something, so these letters are laid around the one that follows

parts.note: the clue's own A begins the word
a street is a way, and ST is its abbreviation
r is the dictionary abbreviation for rare
o is the usual abbreviation for old
a university teacher is a don

explanation.walkthrough: 'Describe' is geometry rather than English here — the sense in which a compass describes an arc — and the elderly academic keeps you reading it as speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Astrodon was a Cretaceous sauropod named for its star-shaped teeth, so 'dinosaur' defines it by class; the name is the obscure half.

clue.text: Surplus of clothing size to be picked up

indicators.note: to pick something up is to catch it by ear, so what matters is the sound of the letters and not their spelling

parts.note: the smallest label size is XS, and those two letters said aloud run together as the answer

explanation.walkthrough: The size on a garment label is written, never spoken, so the clue's whole trick is asking you to say two ordinary letters out loud.
explanation.definitionFit: An excess is the amount over what was needed, which is the leftover a surplus names — though excess also carries a sense of too much that surplus lacks.
